summaries.example: Imagine a weather app that usually says “sunny” or “rainy.” Sometimes the information is not finished, so it might say “unknown.” A many-valued logic adds such extra possibilities instead of forcing every statement into only true or false. Different rules can explain how “unknown” behaves when statements are joined with “and,” “or,” or “not.”
summaries.summary: Classical logic treats each statement as True or False. Many-valued logic asks whether this two-choice system is always enough. It studies systems with three, four, or even infinitely many possible values. An extra value might mean “neither true nor false,” “both true and false,” “unknown,” or a degree between completely false and completely true. The meaning is not fixed by the number alone. We must also decide how connectives such as “and,” “or,” and “not” work, and how to decide whether a conclusion follows from its premises. Some systems are useful for incomplete information, contradictions, vague words such as “old,” or statements whose status is not settled. The entry also explains that many-valued logic is not just about counting values. The rules for reasoning are equally important. Two systems can use the same values but accept different inferences. Some systems use a scale of values from 0 to 1, as in fuzzy logic, while others arrange values in a more complex pattern. Many-valued methods can also be used in computer reasoning and in richer kinds of logic involving quantities or possibilities.
key_ideas: Classical logic usually uses two values: True and False.
Many-valued logics can add a value for uncertainty, missing information, contradiction, or a degree of truth.
There is no single correct way to use an extra value; its meaning and the rules for connectives matter.
Some systems use three or four values, while others use many values along a scale from 0 to 1.
Changing the values or the rules can change which conclusions count as valid.
summaries.why_it_matters: Real information is not always neat. A computer may receive missing data, conflicting reports, or words with blurry meanings. Many-valued logic gives logicians different tools for describing these situations instead of pretending that every sentence fits perfectly into True or False. It also teaches an important lesson: the way we label information and the rules we use to reason with it both affect our conclusions.

important_terms.definition: A system for checking how statements support one another.
The idea that every statement must be exactly True or exactly False.
A logic that uses more possible values than just True and False, or studies truth values in a broader way.
A possible status between True and False, such as neither true nor false, both, or partly true.

questions_to_think_about: Should an unfinished answer be called false, or should it receive a different status?
What should happen if one source says a fact is true and another says it is false?
Which rules should “and,” “or,” and “not” follow when information is incomplete?

summaries.example: Suppose a database receives two reports about proposition p: one says p is true and another says p is false. In classical logic, p and not-p together can imply any conclusion through the principle of explosion. A four-valued system can instead represent p as both true and false while keeping an unrelated proposition q undecided. In the Belnap–Dunn style of reasoning described in the entry, the contradiction about p does not by itself force q to be accepted.
summaries.summary: Many-valued logic generalizes the two-valued, truth-functional framework of classical propositional logic. Classical valuations assign 0 or 1 to atomic formulas and calculate the values of compounds by fixed operations. Many-valued systems enlarge the value set and then make several independent choices: how connectives operate, which values count as designated, and what counts as valid consequence. These choices explain why simply adding a third value does not produce one unique logic. In strong Kleene-style systems, the third value can represent a gap, such as an undefined computation or an indeterminate sentence. In paraconsistent readings, it can represent a glut, allowing a sentence and its negation to be accepted without trivializing the whole system. Four-valued semantics separate the dimensions of support for truth and support for falsity, yielding the statuses True, False, Neither, and Both. This is useful for incomplete or inconsistent information. Other systems order values by degrees of truth, as in fuzzy logics over the real interval [0,1]. Gödel, product, and Łukasiewicz logics use different operations, so their implication and conjunction behave differently. The entry also distinguishes truth-functional many-valuedness from broader semantic ideas. Supervaluations assign a sentence a determinate status across several precise interpretations; nondeterministic semantics allow a connective several possible outputs; and two-dimensional matrices track acceptance and rejection separately. Finally, the same general ideas extend to first-order quantifiers and modal operators, although the resulting systems can have substantially different proof-theoretic and computational properties.
key_ideas: Many-valued logic developed partly from doubts about bivalence, including problems involving future claims, vagueness, presupposition, computation, and semantic paradoxes.
Three-valued systems may use a middle value for a gap, a glut, or another status; the same tables can receive different interpretations and yield different consequence relations.
Four-valued systems can represent True, False, Neither, and Both. Their values need not form a single linear scale.
Fuzzy logics use a continuum such as the interval from 0 to 1, often interpreting values as degrees of truth and distinguishing different conjunction or implication operations.
Logical consequence depends not only on the values and connective tables but also on which values are designated and how preservation is defined.
Many-valued semantics can be generalized through supervaluations, nondeterministic operations, two-dimensional acceptance and rejection, and extensions to first-order and modal logic.
summaries.why_it_matters: Many-valued logic shows that “valid reasoning” is partly shaped by how information is represented. Classical logic remains a central reference point, but it can behave poorly with inconsistency, partial information, vagueness, or graded judgments. Alternative systems make these distinctions explicit and let researchers compare their inferential consequences. This matters in philosophy, formal language, computer science, and the study of reasoning systems, while also warning us that no extra truth value has a meaning or behavior independent of the surrounding semantics.

important_terms.definition: The classical principle that every sentence has exactly one of two values: True or False.
A system in which formulas receive values from a set containing more than two possibilities, often with truth-functional operations.
A missing truth status: a sentence is treated as neither true nor false.
A conflict status: a sentence is treated as both true and false.
A structure containing an algebra of values and a selected set of designated values used to define consequence.
A rule for evaluating a compound formula from the values of its parts.
A relation of following from premises to conclusions, defined by a chosen preservation rule.
A logic that tolerates contradictions without making every statement follow from them.

questions_to_think_about: Does representing a sentence as both true and false describe a contradiction, or merely conflicting information?
Why might a logic reject the law of excluded middle while another rejects explosion?
If truth comes in degrees, should conjunction be minimum, multiplication, or another operation?
Can a bivalent description reproduce the inferences of a many-valued logic without preserving its truth-functional structure?
What should quantifiers mean when different objects receive different truth degrees?

summaries.example: A school database stores whether each student has returned a form. For Alex it knows “yes,” for Bea it knows “no,” and for Casey the form is missing. A two-valued system must call Casey’s statement true or false, but a three-valued system can mark it “unknown.” A different system might use an extra value when two offices give opposite answers. The database’s rules for combining “unknown” with “yes” and “no” will determine which conclusions are safe.
summaries.summary: Many-valued logic begins with a question about classical logic: must every statement be exactly True or exactly False? The principle that says yes is bivalence. Many-valued logics challenge or generalize it by allowing additional statuses. A third value may stand for a truth-value gap, where a sentence is neither true nor false, or for a glut, where it is both. These readings are not interchangeable, because the same-looking tables can support different rules of inference. Four-valued systems make the possibilities especially clear: a claim can be true only, false only, neither, or both. This is helpful when information is incomplete or contradictory. For example, a computer collecting reports may need to record that one claim has support and opposition without allowing an unrelated claim to follow automatically. Other systems treat truth as a degree on a scale from 0 to 1. Fuzzy logics use such values to model partial truth, but they still need precise operations for connectives. One system may define “and” using the smaller degree; another may use multiplication or a special operation. The entry emphasizes that consequence is a separate choice. A logical system must say which values count as designated and how premises and conclusions preserve them. It also discusses broader approaches, including supervaluations for several precise interpretations, nondeterministic semantics where a connective can have more than one allowed output, and extensions to first-order and modal logic. Thus, “many-valued” names a family of approaches, not one single theory.
key_ideas: Classical logic uses two values, but many-valued logic studies systems with three, four, or infinitely many values.
Different three-valued logics can interpret the middle value as unknown, neither true nor false, both true and false, or even unusable information.
Four-valued systems distinguish four combinations: true only, false only, neither, and both.
Some logics use a continuous range from 0 to 1 to represent degrees of truth; these are often called fuzzy logics.
A logic’s conclusions depend on more than its list of values. Its connective rules and its definition of validity also matter.
Many-valued ideas can help with vague language, incomplete databases, paradoxes, and reasoning about possibility or necessity.
summaries.why_it_matters: Everyday and scientific information can be incomplete, vague, or inconsistent. Many-valued logic offers ways to represent these features directly. It also helps us compare different ideas about what it means for a conclusion to follow. Studying these systems shows why logical rules are not just labels: changing the meaning of an extra value or the way validity is defined can change which arguments are accepted.

important_terms.definition: The view that every statement has exactly one of two values, True or False.
A logic that allows several truth statuses or truth degrees instead of only True and False.
A status used when a claim is not settled as true or false.
A status used when a claim is supported as both true and false.
A table or rule that tells how a connective changes the values of its inputs.
The relation that says which conclusions follow from which premises.
Values selected as counting as acceptable or true for a particular way of defining consequence.
A logic designed to reason without automatically turning a contradiction into every conclusion.

questions_to_think_about: Is “unknown” the same as “false”? Why might a logic keep them apart?
Why could a computer need to preserve a contradiction instead of concluding everything?
Should a statement that is 0.6 true and another that is 0.6 true make an “and” statement that is 0.6 true?
Can two logics use the same truth values but disagree about an inference?
What might be gained, and what might become harder, when a logic has infinitely many values?
